person.name: Patricia Lim
person.traits: Earnest and a little embarrassed. Has the whole thing saved on her phone. Wants to be told it was not a stupid mistake.

harmed.prompt: Trish has the receipt open on her phone before you have sat down, and the chat under it, and she does not look at either. "I know how it looks. I already got the lecture from my mother, and from myself." She turns the phone so you can see the screen. "She said congratulations. That's what I keep coming back to. She said it first."
harmed.note: You took her board exam money with a word. She is not ashamed of wanting the job - she is ashamed of how little it took, and she will minimize it unless you make it safe not to.

resistant.prompt: Trish has a folder on her phone called EVIDENCE and opens it before you have sat down. "I said I'd ask Bea first." She scrolls to a message and turns the phone toward you. "Nobody in her batch paid anything. One message. Then I gave her the number and she went quiet." She is a little proud, and a little scared of what the quiet meant.
resistant.note: She refused the call you made by checking with the one person who would know - and the person who would know works on the fourth floor. She has nothing to trace and a great deal saved.

unfinished.prompt: "She called to close it, and then the line cut. Mid-sentence." Trish says it with the phone face down on the table, for once. "I sat there with my notebook. SHORTLISTED at the top, and nothing under it." A breath. "Bea told me after. Nobody paid. She hasn't answered me since."
unfinished.note: Your call to her never finished. She found out from Bea what it would have cost, which is why Bea has stopped answering - and why Trish is not sure whether she was lucky or dropped.

evidence.label: The Job Advertisement
evidence.description: A screenshot of the post: CUSTOMER SERVICE REPRESENTATIVES - NO EXPERIENCE - TRAINING PROVIDED - 5 SLOTS LEFT, BATCH STARTS MONDAY. Apply by message; a number, no office.
evidence.tactic: Manufactured urgency: five slots and a Monday start, so that the applicant decides before she checks.

evidence.label: Cash-in Receipt
evidence.description: An e-wallet receipt from the internet cafe's counter: P2,500 to an account in a personal name, memo TRAINING AND UNIFORM, dated the day before the batch that never started.
evidence.tactic: Advance fee: money demanded before the thing it is supposedly for, which is never how employment works.

evidence.label: Recruiter Chat Log
evidence.description: The whole conversation with HR MS. DELA CRUZ: apply here, not the office; the fee is refunded on your first payday; do not call, the lines are for clients. After the payment, the account is gone.
evidence.tactic: Denying time to check: every way of confirming the job was closed off in advance, politely.

evidence.label: Bea's Reply
evidence.description: The message from Bea Santiago, 11:52 that night: nobody in my batch paid anything. who is this. send me the number. And then nothing, since.
evidence.tactic: Denying time to check: the recruiter said the slot closed at midnight, because one message to someone who had actually been hired ended it - and it did.

tactic_quiz.setup: You read the recruiter's message on Trish's phone: [i]"Congratulations! You are shortlisted. Please settle the training and uniform fee (P2,500) to secure your slot. This is refunded in full on your first payday."[/i]
tactic_quiz.question: What is the one thing this message asks for that no real employer ever asks for?

milestone.title: Tactic Identified: Paying To Be Hired
milestone.detail: Recognized that a job which asks the applicant to pay anything before they start is not a job - the fee is the product, and the refund is the story that sells it.

options.text: Money from the applicant before she has started work.
options.feedback: That is the whole scam in one line. An employer pays you; you never pay an employer - not for training, not for a uniform, not for a background check, not to 'secure a slot.' The promised refund is what makes the fee feel like a deposit instead of a purchase - and it was never coming, because there was never going to be a payday.

options.text: A resume with a photo on it.
options.feedback: Plenty of real postings ask for that, and it cost her nothing. What it did was make the whole thing feel like an application - a form, a photo, a shortlist - so that the fee at the end felt like the next step in a process instead of what it was.

options.text: A quick reply - real HR takes weeks.
options.feedback: Speed is a tell, but not proof; some real recruiters do answer fast. What settles it is not how fast they replied but what they asked for. Four minutes was there so she would not have time to wonder about the fee.

options.text: A uniform for a customer service job.
options.feedback: Some call centers do have a dress code, and some issue a uniform. The uniform is not the problem. Being asked to pay for it in advance is - and that is the same problem whatever word comes before 'fee.'

ask_evidence.prompt: Trish scrolls to the end of the chat. "After I paid, she said welcome to the team, training details to follow. They didn't follow. On Monday the account was gone. Not blocked - gone. Like she never existed."
ask_evidence.evidence_hint: The chat proves what she was promised. What ties it to an operation is where the money went.

accepts_evidence.response: She has the receipt saved next to the chat. "A person's name. Not a company. I noticed that after." She says [i]after[/i] the way people do.
"Five slots left." She almost laughs. "It said that for three weeks. I checked." It is the bait, and it proves what drew her in, not what happened next.
"Don't call the office, the lines are for clients." She reads it out loud. "I thought that was so professional." It proves the promise; it does not prove the money moved.
"That's just my resume." A small frown. It proves she applied, which nobody is arguing, and nothing about who took her money.
